subject: Chemistry
title: Radioactive Decay: Atoms That Fall Apart
description: A 60-second lesson on Radioactive Decay: Atoms That Fall Apart.

hook.text: Some atoms are unstable. They spontaneously emit particles and energy to reach a more stable state—that's radioactive decay.

buildup.text: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 when uranium salts fogged a photographic plate in the dark.

discovery.text: Three types of decay: alpha (emits a helium nucleus), beta (emits an electron), and gamma (emits pure energy).

twist.text: Each isotope has a unique half-life—the time for half the atoms to decay. It ranges from microseconds to billions of years.

climax.text: Uranium-238 decays through 14 steps over 4.5 billion years before finally becoming stable lead-206.

punchline.text: Unstable atoms shed particles until they find peace. Nature's slow countdown.

quiz.question: What are the three types of radioactive decay?
options: Proton emission, neutron emission, and electron capture

details.summary: Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable atomic nucleus releases energy by emitting alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays. The process is spontaneous and probabilistic, governed by half-lives that range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
details.whyItMatters: Radioactive decay powers nuclear energy, enables medical imaging and cancer treatment, drives geological dating, and explains why Earth's interior remains hot after 4.5 billion years.
takeaways: Unstable nuclei decay by emitting alpha, beta, or gamma radiation
Half-life is the time for half the atoms in a sample to decay
Decay is random for individual atoms but statistically predictable

faq.question: What determines whether an atom is radioactive?
faq.answer: The ratio of protons to neutrons determines nuclear stability. Too many or too few neutrons relative to protons creates instability. The strong nuclear force must overcome proton-proton repulsion; when it cannot, the nucleus decays to reach a more stable configuration.

faq.question: Can you predict exactly when a specific atom will decay?
faq.answer: No. Radioactive decay is fundamentally random at the individual atom level. You can only predict the probability that a given atom decays within a time period. For large samples, the statistical behavior is extremely predictable through the half-life equation.
